lines: A pharmacist in Adelaide made this guide.
When you see the word **we**, it means the pharmacist who runs this website.
We wrote this information in an easy to read way.
We use pictures to explain some ideas.
We wrote some important words in **bold**.
This means the letters are thicker and darker.
We explain what these words mean in the word list at the end.
This is an Easy Read summary of our website.
It only has the most important ideas.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
You can ask for help to read this guide.
A friend, family member, support person or your pharmacist may be able to help you.
Some trans and gender diverse people take **hormone medicines**.
These medicines change your body over time.
Doctors call this **gender-affirming hormone therapy**.
People often have questions about these medicines, like:
- how much they cost
- what to do when a chemist has none left
- how to use them safely.
The answers are usually written for doctors and pharmacists.
They can be hard to find and hard to read.
We made this guide to help.
This guide does not tell you what medicine to take.
Your doctor or nurse practitioner decides that with you.
First you see a doctor or nurse practitioner.
If they agree the medicine is right for you, they write a **prescription**.
A prescription is a note that lets you get the medicine.
Then you take the prescription to a pharmacy.
A pharmacy is also called a chemist.
It helps to use the same pharmacy each time.
The staff get to know you.
They can order your medicine in before you run out.
Your medicine label might show a name you do not use.
This is because the pharmacy computer uses your Medicare name.
You can ask the pharmacy to put your **preferred name** on the label.
Your preferred name is the name you want people to use.
Some staff will not know how to do this straight away.
They may need to ring the people who make their computer program.
It is okay to ask them to find out.

sections.h: When a medicine is hard to get

lines: Sometimes a medicine runs out across the whole country.
This is called a **shortage**.
It is not your fault and it is not your pharmacy's fault.
Our website checks the official shortage list every day.
It shows which hormone medicines are hard to get right now.
If your medicine is hard to get:
- talk to your pharmacist early
- do not wait until you have run out
- ask them to order some in for you.
Your pharmacist may be able to give you a different **brand**.
A different brand is the same medicine in a different box.
This is safe and normal.
The government pays for most of the cost of many medicines.
This is called the **PBS**.
You pay the rest. This part is called a **co-payment**.
Most people pay up to **$25.00** for a PBS medicine.
If you have a concession card, you pay up to **$7.70**.
If you buy a lot of medicine in one year, the cost goes down.
This is called the **Safety Net**.
Ask your pharmacy to keep a record for you.
Some medicines are not on the PBS.
These cost more.
The website has a page that explains each one.
If the cost is too much, tell your pharmacist.
They can often help.
You are not the first person to ask.
Take your medicine the way your doctor told you.
Take it at about the same time each day.
Some medicines are patches or gels that go on your skin.
Some are tablets you swallow.
Some are injections.
If you are not sure how to use your medicine, ask your pharmacist.
You can ask to talk somewhere private.
If you feel unwell after taking your medicine, get help.
Ring your doctor.
In an emergency, ring **000**.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
It has a page for each medicine.
You can ring **healthdirect** on **1800 022 222** to talk to a nurse.
This is free and open all day and all night.
You can tell us if something on the website is wrong or missing.
We want to fix it.
